t: 2830. Maximize the Profit as the Salesman
o: Houses 0..n−1 lie on a line; each buyer offers gold for a contiguous range [start,end], and ranges sold must be disjoint. Maximize total gold. Example 1: sell [0,0] (1) and [1,3] (2) → 3; Example 2: selling [0,2] for 10 beats everything → 10. Classic weighted interval scheduling: dp[i] = best gold using houses < i. Process offers grouped by end: dp[end+1] = max(dp[end], max over offers ending at end of gold + dp[start]).
k: dp[i] = maximum gold achievable using only houses 0..i−1.
Each offer (s,e,g) gives transition dp[e+1] = max(dp[e+1], g + dp[s]).
Grouping offers by end lets one O(n+m) sweep handle everything; binary search over sorted ends is an alternative.

a.n: Approach 1: House-indexed DP with offers bucketed by end
a.i: Sort offers by end, then sweep house positions 1..n carrying dp forward; when reaching position e+1, fold in all offers ending at e.
s: dp[0]=0; for i in 1..n: dp[i]=dp[i−1], then relax each offer with end i−1.
a.t: O(n log n + n + m) — sorting offers, then a linear sweep folding each offer once.

a.n: Approach 2: Offer-indexed DP with binary search
a.i: Sort offers by end; dp[i] = best using the first i offers = max(dp[i−1], goldᵢ + dp[t]) where t = number of offers with end < startᵢ, found by binary search. Handy when n is huge but the offer count is small.
s: For each offer, binary-search the count of strictly earlier-ending offers.
a.t: O(m log m + m log m) — sorting plus a binary search per offer.

w: Prefer approach 1 when n is comparable to m (simplest, cache-friendly); prefer approach 2 when n ≫ m. Pitfall: overlapping offers must be exclusive — dp[start] (houses before start), not dp[start+1]. Follow-up: weighted intervals with weights updated dynamically, or maximize count of sales instead of gold.
